en: The *Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā*, composed by the great scholar and unattached master Kuladatta. 1–4. Examination of the Ground. In this regard, on an auspicious day, lunar mansion, and so forth, preceded by worship, the examination of the ground (*bhūmiparīkṣā*) should be performed.
1–4–1. Grounds to be Abandoned: If the ground is possessed of undesirable trees and the like, then it should be abandoned.

Furthermore, that ground upon which, in sequence from the eastern direction onwards, there stand respectively the *aśvattha*, *arjuna*, *plakṣa*, *palāśa*, *nyagrodha*, *śālmalī*, *bakula*, and *udumbara* trees along with thorny trees, is one that brings about the defects of separation from sons, wife, or wealth; fear of enemies; loss of property; misconduct by a wife; abandonment by attendants; and the destruction of grains such as rice. Therefore, it should be avoided. As it has been said: "One should plant the *vaṭa* tree in the east (Aindrī), and the *udumbara* in the south; one may place the *pippala* in the west."
Likewise, one should plant auspicious Plakṣa trees in the northern directions; however, if these [other trees] are situated in reverse positions, it results in the opposite effect.
Thus:

[2] Furthermore, those lands which have shapes resembling a staff, a cart, the sun, a serpent, a tortoise, a bow, a large-mouthed drum, a muraja drum, a triangle, a fan, a mud-pit, or a hole, and which are uneven and extensive, indeed bestow the faults of the destruction of cattle, wealth, and grain; eye diseases, imprisonment, and oppression; fear of thieves and fire; the loss of property, women, and fear of kings; the loss of wealth, poverty, sorrow, and various afflictions.

[3] Furthermore, those regions belonging to Fire, Yama, Rakṣas, Water, Wind, and the Directions, as well as those floating [in the sky], invariably cause burning, death, disease, poverty, and the increase of enemies.

[4] And that ground which has the sound of dogs, jackals, camels, or broken vessels brings about inauspiciousness. [5] Moreover, that which smells of fat, oil, lye, or birds yields undesirable results.
[6] Ground that is near a sacrificial site, a cremation ground, or many caves and ravines should be avoided.
Furthermore, ground where there are serpent pools, shrines, hermitages, or temples of deities is also censured.
[7] And on a mountain, wherever there are thorny trees, creepers, branches, or withered trees in the cardinal or intermediate directions, that ground is likewise unfavorable.
1-4-2 Characteristics of Auspicious Grounds and Their Auspicious Signs:
[1] Those that are infinite, auspicious, elongated, circular, or square bestow the accomplishment of unfulfilled goals, increase intelligence, and grant wealth and grain.
[2] Furthermore, those that slope toward the east, north, or northeast are glorious and bring about happiness.

And in that region of the Rasa river, in its northern part, there is a lake adorned with clusters of white and red blossoming lotuses, covered with an abundance of flowers such as blue lotuses, water lilies, and fragrant lilies, especially crowded with flocks of various birds, filled with fish, tortoises, and other creatures, and always provided with green grass.
In the eastern quarter there are mango, rose-apple, and kadamba trees; in that very region are the flowering shrubs such as the javā, bandhūka, and āmlā, as well as all those with red blossoms.
Likewise, in the southern direction there are punnāga, nāgakesara, pārijātaka, campaka, and aśoka trees, and especially bakula trees.
In that interval, there are trees fragrant with jasmine, *kunda*, and *mallikā* flowers, as well as all those shrubs with white blossoms;
likewise, in the western direction, there are *pippala*, *udumbara*, *lakucha*, and *panasa* trees— all such milky trees (*kṣīrataru*) are commended when situated in the west.
In that interval, branches with black blossoms are praised.
Moreover, in general, the ground should be one that produces prosperity, characterized by the sounds of lutes, flutes, bulls, and drums.
Specifically, however, the earth should be accepted according to its suitability for the lineage.
For example: those that are white in color, with the fragrance of curd, milk, ghee, and so forth, and possessing a sweet taste, are suitable for Brāhmaṇas.
Those that are red in color, with the fragrance of jasmine, lotus, water-lily, campaka, nāgakesara, and so forth, and possessing an astringent taste, are for Kṣatriyas.
Those that are yellow in color, with the fragrance of wine and elephant ichor, and possessing a sour taste, are for Vaiśyas.
That which is dark-colored, odorless, and pungent-bitter in taste belongs to the Śūdras.
Having dug a pit one cubit deep and filled it with that very same earth, those [stones] which remain level—neither deficient nor excessive—are classified as inferior, superior, or middling.
Alternatively, having excavated a square pit measuring two cubits and fashioned a mandala in its center, one should place a white-colored flower in the eastern direction.
In this manner, one should place red, yellow, and blue flowers in the western, northern, and southern directions respectively.
That among these which does not wither is suitable for that purpose.

In that very pit, in the eastern and other directions, one should kindle lamps upon unbaked jars placed over baked saucers using wicks of white and other colors and clarified butter from a cow, and examine them.
In that regard, if a white wick burns, then that ground is suitable for Brāhmaṇas.
Likewise, in due order, such ground belongs to Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras according to whether the wick is red, yellow, or black.
Similarly, ground abounding in Kuśa grass, Śara grass, Uśīra root, and Dūrvā grass is suitable for Brāhmaṇas and the other classes respectively.
[5] According to some, cities and the like are determined to be on the northern banks of great rivers; according to others, they are determined to be on the southern banks.
1-4-3 (The case where a suitable location cannot be found).
Thus, in the absence of earth possessing the characteristics as previously described, one should perform the acquisition by producing earth of its own kind from whatever has been obtained.

3-3. Following the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the flask, once the maṇḍala has been duly constructed and fully worshipped with the five types of offerings (*pañcopacāra-pūjā*), one should consecrate the flasks.
3-3-1. Regarding that, there are three options: fifty-three, eleven, or five [flasks].
3-3-1-1 The Fifty-three-Person Group: In the fifty-three-person group, there are fifty-four [vases], consisting of a separate *sarvakarmika* (all-purpose) vase for each of all the mandala deities.
3-3-1-2 The Eleven-Person Group: In the eleven-person group, there is one [vase] for the five beginning with Mahāvairocana and Sattvavajrī;
and one [vase] for the five beginning with Akṣobhya.
One from among the five beginning with Ratnasambhava;
one from among the five beginning with Amitābha;
and one from among the five beginning with Amoghasiddhi.
One for each of the four [deities] beginning with Lāsyā;
one for each of the four [deities] beginning with Dhūpa;
and one for each of the five [deities] beginning with Vajrāṅkuśa and Maitreya.
One from among the five beginning with Vajrapāśa and Gandhahastin;
one from among the five beginning with Vajrasphoṭa and Amitaprabha;
and one from among the five beginning with Vajrāveśa and Vajragarbha.
Together with the *sārvakarmika* vase, there are twelve.

Regarding the fivefold system (*pañcapakṣa*): in the fivefold system, there is one [vase] for the nine deities consisting of the five Tathāgatas such as Vairocana and the four goddesses such as Sattvavajrī;
and there is one [vase] for the eight goddesses beginning with Lāsyā.
One [mudrā] for the sixteen bodhisattvas beginning with Vajrasattva;
one for the sixteen bodhisattvas beginning with Maitreya;
and one for the four wrathful deities beginning with Vajrāṅkuśa.

There are six [vessels] including the all-purpose vessel (*sārvakarmikakalaśa*). 3-3-2 The characteristics of the all-purpose vessel: Regarding that, the characteristics of the all-purpose vessel are as follows.
The interior (*garbha*) is forty-nine finger-breadths (*mātrika*) in circumference.
The height up to the edge of the lips is twenty-one mātrās;
the lip hanging below that is two mātrās;
and the mouth cavity is thirteen mātrās.
The cavity of the throat below measures five and a half mātrās;
the height of the neck is eight and a quarter mātrās measured transversely;
and the lower lip is sixteen and a quarter mātrās.

3-3-4 (Meditation): Thereafter, one should meditate upon [the pitchers] filled with water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*), the five jewels, medicinal herbs, grains, and perfumes; their mouths adorned with shining sprouts and their necks wrapped in garlands and cloth; beautified by banners, parasols, golden *tilaka* marks, two-eyed [images], and red lac as sacred threads; their interiors filled with parched grain (*lāja*), unbroken rice (*akṣata*), safflower, *phalinī*, and betel nuts; seated upon cushions made of fresh *darbha* grass; and protected by *dūrvā* grass, *kunda* flowers, cow dung, and white mustard seeds consecrated with the *sārvakarmika* mantra.

Therein, the preceptor, remaining in meditative equipoise, should instantly visualize a flask made of various jewels transformed from the syllable *vaṃ*, situated within a white source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*) arisen from the syllable *āḥ*.

Following that, having contemplated his respective deity through the transformation of its own seed-syllable and emblem, he should summon the knowledge-being (*jñānasattva*) with the hooks of light rays from the seed-syllable at his own heart; having seen it before him, he should offer water for the feet, water for rinsing the mouth, and so forth.

Having caused it to enter the pledge-being (*samayasattva*), he should contemplate that [the pledge-being] has melted through great passion and become nectar in the form of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
One should contemplate the pledge deity (samayadevatā) as having become one with the gnosis deity (jñānadevatā) within the [central] mark.

Then, having grasped the five-stranded thread—ending with a flower garland attached to a vajra—with the left fist together with a vajra-bell, one should consecrate it three times with the heart mantra of the Lord of the Mandala, *oṃ sarvatathāgatamahāyogīśvara hūṃ*, and with the all-purpose mantra, *oṃ vajrayakṣa hūṃ*. Furthermore, having cast three flowers consecrated with that very *vajrayakṣa* mantra, [one should proceed].
One should recite one’s own respective mantra one hundred and eight times.

Thereafter, having worshipped the victory-pots (*vijayaghaṭa*) and others with flowers and other offerings, having sprinkled them with the water from the all-purpose flask (*sārvakarmikakalaśa*), and having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*), one should ring the bell while preceded by the praise beginning with "O you who pervade all...
[and] "O Jina, Lord of the Sugatas, supreme pinnacle of existence, all-pervading one."
O Great King Vairocana of the triple world, homage be to you!
Homage to you, Vajrasattva; homage to you, Vajraratna.
Homage to you, Vajradharma; homage to you, Vajrakarman.
[2] Then, having taken a little water from each of those vases, one should pour it into the *sārvakarmika* (all-purpose) vase.

For whichever master lacks firm conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the Vajradhātu, there is no contradiction in performing all the ritual actions—from the purification of the ground to the consecration—by means of firm conviction in his own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
3-3-5. The Installation of the Vases: Now, the installation of the vases is described.
There, beginning from the eastern gate of the mandala and proceeding clockwise, one should place the victory flask (vijayakalaśa) and the others, ending with the Akṣobhya flask.

At the eastern gate is the victory flask of the Lord of the Mandala (Cakreśa); following that sequence, there are thirteen flasks for Vajrāṅkuśa, Vajrarāga, Vajrasādhu, Sarvāpāyañjaha, Sarvaśokatamonirghātanamati, Vajralāsyā, Sattvavajrī, Vajradhūpā, Gandhahasti, Śūraṅgama, Vajratejas, and Vajraratna.

Thus, beginning from the southern gate, there are thirteen vases for Ratnasaṃbhava, Vajrapāśa, Vajraketu, Vajrahāsa, Gaganagañja, Jñānaketu, Vajramālā, Ratnavajrī, Vajrapuṣpa, Amitaprabha, Candraprabha, Vajratīkṣṇa, and Vajradharma. Likewise, beginning from the western gate, [there are vases] for Amitābha, Vajrasphoṭa, Vajrahetu, Vajrabhāṣa, Bhadrapāla, Jālinīprabha, Vajragītā, Dharmavajrī, Vajradīpa, Vajragarbha, Akṣayamati, Vajrarakṣa, and Vajrakarma.

There are thirteen vases. Likewise, beginning from the northern gate, there are fourteen vases for Amoghasiddhi, Vajrāveśa, Vajrayakṣa, Vajrasandhi, Pratibhānakūṭa, Samantabhadra, Vajranṛtyā, Karmavajrī, Vajragandhā, Maitreya, Amoghadarśin, Vajrarāja, Vajrasattva, and Akṣobhya.
The *sārvakarmika* flask, however, should be placed in the northeast corner, within the row of flasks, with respect to the outer directions.

Thus, having caused each of the previously consecrated flasks to circumambulate the mandala circle clockwise, the placement of the flasks is to be performed outside the mandala circle, beyond the perimeter wall (*cakravāḍa*) and the garland of flames of the ground.
Furthermore, at the time of the deposition of the flasks, the Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* should be recited.
One should also worship the maṇḍala with incense burners containing camphor, agallochum, turuṣka, and other aromatics, as well as lamps and so forth.

3–5. Laying the Lines (Sūtrapātana) 3–5–1. First, five sets of five lines are consecrated. Then, the preceptor, possessing the yoga of the Lord of the Maṇḍala, having taken refuge in all the Tathāgatas in the sky and worshipped them, [takes] five sets of five threads spun by a virgin (*kanyā*) or purchased from a hero (*vīra*). These threads have been dyed individually with white, yellow, red, green, and black pigments, and are produced from the seed-syllables of the five Tathāgatas: *vuṃ*, *āṃ*, *jrīṃ*, *khaṃ*, and *hūṃ*.
One should consecrate with those very [mantras].

3-5-2 One should then supplicate the five Tathāgatas. Thereafter, having visualized the wisdom threads consisting of rays of light produced from seed-syllables such as *vūṃ* within the hearts of the five Tathāgatas situated in space, one says:
*oṃ āḥ śāśvata vajrasūtraṃ me prayaccha hūṃ*. (1)
With this, one should supplicate Mahāvairocana.
Likewise: Oṃ Āḥ Ratneśa, grant me the vajra-thread, Hūṃ; (2) Oṃ Āḥ Amitaiśa, grant me the vajra-thread, Hūṃ. (3)
Oṃ āḥ Amogheśa, grant me the vajra-thread, hūṃ.
(4) Oṃ āḥ Citteśa, grant me the vajra-thread, hūṃ. (5) With this [mantra].
One should pray to Ratnaśikhī and the others.
The twenty-five threads are divided; from the syllable *jaḥ*, one whose two eyes have the nature of a yellow moon and sun [visualizes]: *Oṃ dīptadṛṣṭyaṅkuśi jaḥ*. (6)

Having uttered this, with a blazing gaze like a goad that draws in the lashes of her darting, trembling eyes, she should draw in those [threads] sent by Vairocana and the others, and insert them right there within their respective threads of color. For this very reason, those [threads], consisting of the five cognitions beginning with the mirror-like cognition (*ādarśajñāna*), become divided into twenty-five, since each of the cognitions beginning with the mirror-like cognition is followed by four cognitions.

3-5-4 One should wind a single thread; thereafter, in the form of the *sārvakarmika* [thread], together with the ritual master (*karmācārya*) who holds the threads, one should first wind each of the five threads individually using five [threads] each.

Thereafter, with those five [threads] thus wound, [one should wind] a single thread [with the mantra]: *oṃ anyonyānugatāḥ sarvadharmāḥ parasparānupraviṣṭāḥ sarvadharmā atyantānupraviṣṭāḥ sarvadharmāḥ, oṃ āḥ hūṃ*. (7)
Reciting thus, one should rotate [the thread].

3-5-5 The laying of the Brahma-thread: immediately after the rotation, having sat down, placed [the thread] in a vessel made of gold or other materials, worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and incense, and protected it with the Sarvakarmika mantra, [one recites]:
*Oṃ vajrasamayasūtraṃ mātikrama hūṃ*. (8)
With this [mantra], one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*) one hundred and eight times.

Again, having sprinkled [the object] with the water from all the vases while reciting the mantra *oṃ sarvaśodhani hūṃ phaṭ* (nine times), and having scattered flowers, one should visualize the maṇḍala of the chosen deity situated in the expanse of the sky; having worshipped it preceded by the offering of the *argha* water, and having prostrated, one should oneself—

The practitioner, possessing that yoga, visualizes the superior practitioner (uttarasādhaka) in the form of the All-Action (sārvakarmika) deity. Having meditated on the moon and sun—shining yellow and produced from the syllable *jjaḥ*—at his own left and right eyes respectively, he holds the thread with his left vajra-fist at his navel. He then dispatches the superior practitioner, who likewise holds the thread, by means of the three *jjaḥ* syllables: "jjaḥ jjaḥ jjaḥ. Regarding the superior practitioner: "jjaḥ jjaḥ jjaḥ."

Thus, having drawn [the thread] with three *jihvākāra* syllables and positioned it facing the same way, one standing in the western direction facing east and one standing in the southern direction facing north should cast two Brahma-threads into the sky at the level of the navel.
Taking the thread with the fingers of the right hand holding a vajra, one should produce the sound of a snap (*acchaṭā*). And this applies to all instances of casting the threads.
Oṃ vajrasamayasūtraṃ mātikrama hūṃ | hūṃ oṃ āḥ—
thus one should recite.
And by that sound of the thread, one should summon the Tathāgatas who pervade all space;
having arrived, they enter within the threads.
For this sound has a conventional meaning: "The time for you to act for the sake of sentient beings has come; therefore, come here."
In all cases, the preceptor and the assistant preceptor should proceed clockwise;
they should also resolve upon the equality of all directions.
On the ground, two Brahma-lines should be laid out like two lines in the sky, by means of two hands holding cords that hang down equally from both sides.

3-5-6. Laying down the lines for the cardinal directions, the base, and the sides: Then, standing at the *ṭakkika* peg and facing the *vajravidāraṇa* peg, one should lay down the eastern direction line.

Subsequently, standing at the *vajrāntacara* peg and facing the *vajrāṭṭahāsa* peg, one should lay down the eastern base line. Then, standing at the *mahābala-krodha* peg and facing the *ratnaśikhara* peg, one should lay down the western direction line.
Following that, standing at the peg where the footstep was placed and facing the peg of Vajrapālaka, one should drop the western root-line.

Then, standing at the peg of the great wrathful deity Vajrapracaṇḍa and facing the peg of Vajrācala, one should drop the northern directional line. Following that, standing at the peg of Vajrabhīmaka and facing the peg of Vajravidrāpaka, one should drop the northern root-line.
Then, having assumed the form of the great wrathful Vajrapāśa-kīlaka, with the face of the great wrathful Vajrāmṛtakuṇḍali-kīlaka, he should cast the side-line.
Then, having assumed the form of the Vajrāveśa-kīlaka, with the face of the Prajñāntaka-kīlaka, he should cast the side-line.
Following that, standing as the Padmāntaka-kīlaka, with the face of the Vajrāṅkuśa-kīlaka, he should cast the side-line.
Then, standing at the *kīla* of Yamāntaka with the face of the *vajrasphoṭa-kīla*, one should cast the side-line.
For the casting of all the lines, one should go around each one individually in a clockwise direction before casting it.
Then, at the conclusion of casting the lines, situated in the southwest corner and facing northeast, preceded by offerings and worship, [one should proceed].

Reciting "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Vajra Muḥ," one should dismiss the wisdom-thread (*jñānasūtra*), dissolve it into the hearts of the Tathāgatas residing in the sky, and place the five-colored thread in its proper location. This is the procedure for laying the lines. Regarding the signs: according to the statement, "Through signless [actions] there would be no accomplishment; if the thread is broken, there is the ruin of the Guru," one should observe the signs.
The signs are the cutting of the thread, weeping, leaping over the thread, touching the body, the uttering of names, and so forth.
Among these, [1] by the cutting of the thread, the death of the preceptor occurs;
[2] they say that by the howling of dogs, jackals, vultures, and herons, the death of the patron occurs.
[3] When a cat leaps over it, that bone belongs to a donkey;
when a donkey leaps over it, that bone belongs to a dog;
when a dog leaps over it, that bone belongs to a cat.
For the two [types of] leaping, [the meat] of goats and sheep is used; or their bone, or the bone of a cow.
With a horse, the bone of a horse;
with an elephant, the bone of an elephant or the bone of a camel.
That bone [is prepared] with a donkey;
the jackal bone with a buffalo;
the deer bone with a deer.
By means of a bear, the bone of a bear;
by means of a boar, the bone of a tiger;
by means of a tiger, the bone of an elephant.
A mouse-bone by a mouse;
a snake-bone by a snake;
a tortoise-bone by a tortoise.
[4] If anyone among the preceptor, the artisan, the patron, or their appointed agents scratches his head, then there is a shaft (*śalya*) one man’s length below.
If he touches his eyebrows, there is gold or glass at a distance of three cubits. If he touches his eyes, there is a pearl beneath the lower limit of the eye.
If one touches hair or wood on the face, silver is found three finger-breadths below;
from touching a tooth with three hands, a tooth is inferred;
and from scratching the ear, there will be silver, gold, or coral at the end of the ear and below it.

By touching the throat, below that [point] there is a necklace or an iron chain; or, at the lower part of the three-fold arch (trikā), there is the skeleton of a cat. By touching the shoulder, below that [point] there is an ornament corresponding to that [touch].
Upon touching the armpit, there is iron below the armpit.
Upon squeezing the arm, there is an ornament reaching down to the neck.
Upon touching with the right hand, there is a skull or an earthenware bowl reaching down to the waist on the back.
If touched by the left hand, the foot of the bed is one cubit below the knee;
if scratched on the side, there is dust one and a half cubits below;
if touched on the chest, there is the rib-bone of an animal one cubit below the waist.
Upon touching the back, there is a bone in the back, located at a depth equal to its measurement;
upon touching the waist, there is an iron thorn in a region two cubits below;
and by touching the genitals, there is a trident made of three metals at a depth of one cubit.
Upon the touch of the calf, the bone is eleven finger-breadths below;
upon the touch of the ankle, it is eighteen finger-breadths below, like a horse's hoof;
and upon the touch of the foot, it is twelve finger-breadths below, like a thorn of the silk-cotton tree (*śālmalī*).
If the touch is on the little toe of the foot, it is bronze (*kāṃsya*) at a depth of eight finger-breadths;
if the touch is on the heel, it is mica (*abhraka*) at a depth of twelve finger-breadths.

At the time of laying the foundation lines, if the name of a certain living being is recited by another person standing at the side of the patron (*yajamāna*), one may conclude with certainty that the bone of that creature is located there.
[6] If a cow comes unexpectedly and voids dung, it is certain that beneath it there is gold of a corresponding measure.
If a young girl comes unexpectedly and voids excrement, then beneath it there will certainly be silver of a corresponding measure.
From the croaking of frogs, there is danger from water.
The heart-pleasing warbling of parrots, starlings, swans, cuckoos, peacocks, jīvañjīvaka birds, ruddy geese, and bulls brings about auspiciousness.

A sound as pleasing as that of a lion, an elephant, or a thundercloud leads to the acquisition of wealth, grain, and desired objects. Through the sounding of conch shells, auspicious songs, and children’s play, there is the attainment of wealth.
Upon seeing smoke, there is mental distress.
Upon seeing people afflicted by lowliness, wretchedness, or disease, there is illness.
Auspiciousness occurs upon seeing banners, parasols, flags, wine, meat, bells, ornaments, lotuses, curd, molasses, fire-flames, fruits, pairs of fish, kings, women, and so forth.
"May there be Dharma upon the sight of learned Brahmins, mendicants, and virtuous people"—
this is the statement of the omen.
3-5-8 (Drawing the lines).

Thereafter, having performed the laying out of the lines (*sūtrapātana*), the Master, for the sake of increasing the power of the people and the wealth, should take a golden stylus with his right hand holding a vajra and mark the directional lines (*dik-sūtra*) starting from the northeast and proceeding clockwise.
In the same manner, with his left hand holding a bell, he should mark the primary lines (*mūla-sūtra*).
